Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • After a missed 30-day deadline, informal review requests are accepted until June 1, 2026, and adjustments then apply to tax year 2026 only. (Informal Review and Formal Appeal Process (MT DOR); source)
  • Decisions of the Montana Tax Appeal Board are final unless the taxpayer pursues district court action. (Informal Review and Formal Appeal Process (MT DOR); source)
  • Between May 1 and May 30 of the year the redemption period expires, the county treasurer or lien assignee must give notice that a tax deed may issue unless the lien is redeemed. (15-18-212 MCA; source)
  • Notice is by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the current occupant and each party on a litigation guarantee. (15-18-212 MCA; source)

How is Montana property tax calculated?

Montana multiplies the assessed market value by a tax rate to get taxable value, then multiplies taxable value by the local millage rate and divides by 1,000. The Department of Revenue prints the formula on its appraisal notice guide: assessed value times tax rate equals taxable value, and taxable value times millage divided by 1,000 equals general property taxes.

A mill raises $1 for each $1,000 of taxable value. The notice shows the prior year millage total levied by county taxing authorities. Your bill can also include special assessments and fees for items such as solid waste, street lighting and special or rural improvement districts, which the county treasurer can explain.

Value is only half of the story. The department notes that a higher market value on your notice does not mean taxes rise by the same percentage, because tax rates and mill levies move too.

ItemDetail from the Department of Revenue
Current appraisal cycle2025 to 2026, with a market value date of January 1, 2024
Prior appraisal cycle2023 to 2024, with a value date of January 1, 2022
FormulaAssessed value times rate, then times millage divided by 1,000
Bill mailingTypically late October
Payment datesFirst payment November 30, second payment May 31

When are Montana property taxes due, and what happens if you pay late?

Half the tax is due by 5 p.m. on November 30, or within 30 days after the tax notice is postmarked if that is later, and the other half by 5 p.m. on May 31. MCA 15-16-102 sets those dates. If a due date lands on a holiday or Saturday, you can pay without penalty or interest by 5 p.m. the next business day.

Unpaid amounts become delinquent. Interest runs at 5/6 of 1% a month from the delinquency until paid, and a 2% penalty is added. The statute also lets you pay current-year taxes without paying delinquent ones, though payments toward delinquent taxes go to the oldest delinquency first.

A payment plan exists for primary residences. Under the alternative schedule, a homeowner pays one-seventh each month on the last day of the month from November 30 through May 31, on dates of November 30, December 31, January 31, February 28, March 31, April 30 and May 31. Missing a monthly date triggers the usual interest and penalty.

  • Check your bill before closing so the title company has an exact payoff figure.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether any special assessments sit on the bill.
  • Look at whether the house is enrolled for a reduced rate before assuming the standard class rate.

What are the 2026 Montana property tax rates?

The rate depends on how the property is used. For tax year 2026, qualifying primary residences and long-term rentals use a tiered scale starting at 0.76%, while second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay a flat 1.90%.

Property type, 2026Rate
Primary residence or long-term rental, first $378,0000.76%
Same, $378,001 to $756,0000.90%
Same, $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10%
Same, above that1.90%
Second homes, short-term rentals, vacant lots1.90%
Multifamily long-term rentals1.10%
Commercial and industrial under $2,274,0001.50%
Commercial and industrial at or above $2,274,0001.90%
Non-qualified agricultural land14.35%
Qualified agricultural land2.05%
Forest land0.37%

On agricultural or forest parcels, a home and one-acre homesite that is a primary residence or long-term rental takes the tiered residential rate. If it is a second home or short-term rental, the department lists 1.90% on non-qualified agricultural and forest parcels and 1.35% on qualified agricultural parcels. Land of 160 or more acres qualifies automatically as agricultural, and smaller parcels need proof of agricultural use and income.

Which Montana exemptions and relief programs can lower the bill?

The main relief is the Homestead Reduced Rate for owner-occupied principal residences and the Long-Term Rental Reduced Rate for homes rented to tenants for 28 or more days at a time for at least seven months. Homeowners enroll with the Department of Revenue. The application period for 2027 runs from May 4, 2026 to March 1, 2027, and the department verifies enrollment by geocode.

A tax lien notice from the county treasurer must also list the assistance programs on offer. MCA 15-17-125 names the property tax assistance programs under Title 15, chapter 6, part 3, the homestead reduced tax rate, the rental property reduced tax rate, state property tax assistance, and the residential property tax credit for the elderly.

Our Montana homestead exemption guide covers eligibility, enrollment and what changes when you sell. A homeowner who is struggling with a bill should raise these programs with the Department of Revenue or the county treasurer before any lien attaches.

What is a Montana tax lien, and when does it attach?

When real property taxes stay delinquent, the county treasurer must attach a tax lien no later than the first working day in August, provided proper notice was given. Under MCA 15-17-125, the county holds the lien unless it is assigned to a third party, and the treasurer may not attach a lien where proper notice was not given.

The treasurer must mail notice of the pending attachment at least two weeks before the lien attaches. After attaching, the treasurer prepares a tax lien certificate, signs it, files a copy with the county clerk and recorder, and mails a copy to the person assessed.

  • The certificate lists the date the taxes became delinquent and the date the lien attached.
  • It shows the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs separately.
  • It states that the lien may lead to a tax deed and gives the date the county or an assignee becomes entitled to one.

County offices post their own dates. Madison County, for example, says that for 2026 delinquent taxes not received by July 30, 2026 (postmarks are not accepted) will have a tax lien certificate filed on July 31, 2026. The tax deed step comes later, and the notice window of May 1 to May 30 in the redemption year is covered in the section above on official sources.

How should you handle property tax when selling a Montana house?

Pay what is due, get a current payoff from the county treasurer, and let the closing statement settle the rest. A house with a delinquent bill, a lien certificate or a tax deed clock running is still sellable, but the amounts owed come out of the proceeds and the title company will require them.

  • Pull the appraisal notice to confirm the classification and the value the Department of Revenue assigned.
  • Check whether the reduced rate is in place, since it expires at year end after a sale.
  • Call the treasurer for any prior-year delinquency, penalty and interest.
  • If you disagree with the value, remember the review deadlines listed above.

Sellers who face back taxes can talk to Cash Home Buyers about an as-is cash sale. We give general information on this page, not legal or tax advice, and the county treasurer or Department of Revenue can confirm exact figures.

More questions about Montana Property Tax Guide

When are property taxes due in Montana?

Half is due by 5 p.m. on November 30, or within 30 days after the notice is postmarked if later, and the other half by 5 p.m. on May 31. The county treasurer mails bills, typically in late October.

What is the penalty for late Montana property tax?

Delinquent taxes draw interest at 5/6 of 1% per month from the delinquency until paid, and 2% is added as a penalty under MCA 15-16-102.

Can I pay Montana property tax monthly?

Primary residences can use the alternative payment schedule of seven monthly installments from November 30 through May 31, paid by the last day of each month. Missing a date triggers interest and penalty.

What is the Montana property tax rate on a second home in 2026?

1.90% flat, the same rate that applies to short-term rentals and vacant residential lots, according to the Department of Revenue.

When does Montana attach a tax lien?

The county treasurer must attach a lien to delinquent property no later than the first working day in August, after mailing notice at least two weeks earlier (MCA 15-17-125).

How do I check if my Montana home gets the homestead rate?

Use the Department of Revenue Homestead Enrollment Verification Tool with your property geocode, or call 406-444-6900.

title: Montana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home
content:
Montana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Montana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Montana Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Montana Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Montana Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Montana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • The Homestead Reduced Rate lowers property taxes for owners who occupy the Montana home as principal residence at least seven months per year. (Homestead Reduced Tax Rate FAQs (MT DOR); source)
  • Eligibility: owner or revocable grantor trust owns the home, owner is current on property taxes, and no other homestead rate is claimed. (Homestead Reduced Tax Rate FAQs (MT DOR); source)
  • A Montana homestead declaration (creditor protection, filed with the clerk and recorder) is separate from and does not qualify for the Homestead Reduced Rate. (Homestead Reduced Tax Rate FAQs (MT DOR); source)
  • The reduced rate stays with a property through the end of the calendar year after a sale; the buyer must enroll to continue it the next year. (Homestead Reduced Tax Rate FAQs (MT DOR); source)
  • A home not previously enrolled is taxed at a flat 1.9% for 2026 for buyers who miss the deadline, with a refund of the difference available Jan 1-May 31, 2027. (Homestead Reduced Tax Rate FAQs (MT DOR); source)
Selling in Montana?
We buy Montana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Montana homestead exemption actually cover?

Montana uses the word homestead for two separate programs, and sellers often mix them up. One lowers the property tax rate on a home you live in. The other protects home equity from creditors.

The tax program is the Homestead Reduced Rate. According to the Montana Department of Revenue, it applies to owners who occupy their Montana home as a principal residence for at least seven months per year, and it carries a lower rate than standard Class 4 residential property. The creditor protection is a homestead declaration, which is filed with the county clerk and recorder. The department states plainly that a declaration does not qualify you for the reduced rate.

Which one matters depends on why you are selling. If the house is carrying a tax bill you cannot keep up with, the reduced rate is the tool. If a judgment creditor is circling, the declaration is the tool. Many owners need neither, but you should know which one is already attached to the house before you list it or take an offer.

FeatureHomestead Reduced RateHomestead declaration
What it doesLowers the property tax rateProtects equity from creditors
Where it is claimedMontana Department of RevenueCounty clerk and recorder
Residency testPrincipal residence at least seven months a yearDeclaration states you reside on the premises
Who can claimIndividuals, couples, revocable grantor trustsPerson selecting the homestead

Who qualifies for the Homestead Reduced Rate?

You qualify when the home is your principal residence for at least seven months a year, you or your revocable grantor trust own it, you are current on property taxes, and it is the only residence you claim the rate for. Those four conditions come straight from the Department of Revenue FAQ.

The seven months do not have to run back to back. Short absences such as vacations, medical stays or military deployments generally do not cost you eligibility if the home remains your principal residence. Renting the house for a few months does not disqualify it either. The department gives the example of living there from April through December and renting from January to March.

  • Properties owned by an LLC, partnership, corporation or irrevocable trust are not eligible for the homestead rate.
  • If there are several owners, the property qualifies as long as one owner meets the test.
  • Being behind on prior-year taxes disqualifies you. For 2026 taxes, current means paid in full or the first-half payment made.
  • You generally cannot claim the rate while also claiming a homestead in another state.

Homes owned through an LLC or irrevocable trust can still qualify for the separate Long-Term Rental Reduced Rate if they are rented to tenants for 28 or more days at a time, for at least seven months a year, as the tenant's residence.

What are the 2026 tax rates for a Montana homestead?

For tax year 2026, a qualifying homestead is taxed in tiers: 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90% on the next slice up to $756,000, 1.10% from there to $1,511,999, and 1.90% on any portion above that. Each slice is taxed at its own rate, not the whole value at one rate.

Property type (2026)Rate
Homestead, first $378,0000.76%
Homestead, $378,001 to $756,0000.90%
Homestead, $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10%
Homestead, $1,512,000 and above1.90%
Second homes, short-term rentals, vacant residential lots1.90% flat
Multifamily used as long-term rentals1.10% flat

The gap between the homestead tiers and the 1.90% flat rate is why a sale in Montana can change the tax picture. A buyer who will not live in the house, or who plans to run it as a vacation rental, faces the higher flat rate. A buyer who will live there can enroll and expect the lower tiers. The Department of Revenue 2026 page lists the rates.

How do you enroll, and what are the deadlines?

You enroll through the Department of Revenue's Homestead.mt.gov pages, online or by mailed application. The application period for the 2027 tax year runs from May 4, 2026 to March 1, 2027. Enrollment for 2026 closed March 20, 2026.

You attest that the property meets the ownership, use, residency and tax-payment criteria. The department warns that a false attestation can cost you the classification and bring legal and financial penalties.

Some owners do not need to enroll again. If you received the 2025 property tax rebate and still own and live in the same home, the FAQ says you are already enrolled. You must enroll if you moved, no longer use the home as your principal residence, the property was sold or transferred, or ownership changed since the rebate. New construction needs its own application.

  • Check enrollment with the department's Homestead Enrollment Verification Tool, using the property geocode.
  • Find the geocode through the Montana Cadastral site or property.mt.gov by searching the address or owner name.
  • Call the Department of Revenue Call Center at 406-444-6900 or visit a local field office for eligibility questions.

What happens to the reduced rate when you sell?

The reduced rate stays with the property through the end of the calendar year in which it sells, and the buyer must enroll to keep it going into the next year. The department says this directly: the rate expires at year end, and buyers who will use the home as a principal residence need to enroll then.

If the house was not enrolled before the sale, the picture is different. A buyer who closes after the deadline on a home with no prior reduced-rate enrollment is taxed at a flat 1.9% for 2026. That buyer can claim a refund of the difference between the flat rate and the homestead rate between January 1 and May 31, 2027, after paying 2026 taxes in full and filing the refund form.

Timing also matters for people who sell one home and buy another in the same year. The department allows you to combine months of residence if the two homes were occupied consecutively for seven months. If you sold in July and moved into the new house in August, the months count together. If the new home was not occupied until September, they do not.

For a seller, the practical points are short:

  • Confirm whether your house is enrolled before you quote a buyer anything about next year's taxes.
  • Pay every installment that is due so the house is not delinquent when the sale closes.
  • Tell the buyer to enroll as the new owner once the enrollment window is open.

How does a Montana homestead declaration work?

A declaration is a recorded document in which the owner states that they live on the property and claims it as a homestead. Under Montana Code Annotated 70-32-105, the person selecting a homestead must execute and acknowledge the declaration the same way a deed is acknowledged and file it for record. Section 70-32-106 says it must state that the person is residing on the premises and claims them as a homestead, with a description of the premises. Section 70-32-107 requires recording in the county where the land sits.

The protection has a ceiling. Under 70-32-104, the homestead value limit was $350,000 in 2021 and rises 4% each calendar year after that. If you own an undivided interest, your exemption is proportional to your share. Section 70-32-201 makes the homestead exempt from execution or forced sale except as the chapter provides.

Sale proceeds get a limited shelter too. Under 70-32-213, money paid to the claimant from a sale up to the exemption amount keeps the same protection against legal process for 18 months. The Montana courts website offers a homestead declaration form and a form for declaring abandonment of a homestead, both under its estate planning and probate forms page.

If you are selling by choice, a declaration matters most when judgment liens or unpaid bills exist and you want to know how much of the proceeds you may keep. A Montana attorney can confirm how the limit applies to your facts.

What should a Montana seller with tax or creditor pressure do first?

Start by pulling the three facts that drive everything else: whether the house is enrolled for the reduced rate, whether property taxes are current, and whether a declaration was ever recorded.

  • Run the geocode through the enrollment verification tool to see the tax classification.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the current balance and any delinquent amounts, since delinquency also blocks the reduced rate.
  • Search the county clerk and recorder records for a homestead declaration and for judgment liens against the owner.
  • Look at your appraisal notice to see how the Department of Revenue classified the property.

Homes that are vacant, inherited, tenant-occupied or in disrepair often fall outside the reduced rate, so the 1.90% flat rate may already be in the tax bill. A cash buyer can price the house as it stands, and a title company clears recorded items at closing. This is general information, not legal or tax advice. Confirm details with the Department of Revenue or a licensed professional.

More questions about Montana Homestead Exemption

Is the Montana homestead exemption the same as the homestead reduced tax rate?

No. The reduced tax rate lowers your property tax and is claimed through the Montana Department of Revenue. The homestead declaration protects home equity from creditors and is recorded with the county clerk and recorder. The department states that a declaration does not qualify you for the reduced rate.

How long do I have to live in the house to get the Montana homestead rate?

You must occupy it as your principal residence at least seven months each year. The months do not need to be consecutive, and short absences for vacations, medical stays or military deployments generally do not affect eligibility.

Does the homestead rate transfer to the buyer when I sell?

Only for the rest of that calendar year. The reduced rate expires at year end, and the buyer must enroll as the new owner if they will live in the home. A home with no prior enrollment is taxed at a flat 1.9% for 2026, with a refund of the difference available January 1 to May 31, 2027 to a qualifying buyer.

How much equity does a Montana homestead declaration protect?

Under MCA 70-32-104 the limit was $350,000 in 2021 and increases 4% every calendar year after 2021. Co-owners of an undivided interest are limited to a proportional share. Check the current figure with a Montana attorney or the Department of Revenue before relying on a specific number.

title: Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Montana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Montana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Montana no longer collects estate or inheritance taxes. (Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax (MT DOR); source)
  • Montana's inheritance tax was repealed in November 2000 and does not apply to deaths after January 1, 2001. (Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax (MT DOR); source)
  • Estate fiduciaries may need to file Form FID-3 (Montana income tax return for estates and trusts) if federal Form 1041 was filed and the decedent owned Montana property or had Montana-source income. (Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax (MT DOR); source)
  • Montana no longer requires a certificate or consent from the department to close probate or transfer securities. (Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax (MT DOR); source)
Selling in Montana?
We buy Montana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Montana have an estate or inheritance tax?

No. The Montana Department of Revenue states that Montana no longer collects estate or inheritance taxes. The inheritance tax was repealed in November 2000 and does not apply to deaths after January 1, 2001, and Montana has no estate tax for deaths after 2004.

For heirs, that means no Montana death tax return stands between a house and its sale. The department also says Montana no longer requires a certificate or consent from it to close probate or transfer securities. Other costs can still arise, so the sections below walk through them.

Is there a federal estate tax that could reach a Montana house?

Only for large estates. The IRS lists a basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000 for people who die in 2026, and an annual gift exclusion of $19,000 per recipient for gifts made in 2026.

ItemAmountSource
Montana inheritance taxRepealed; none for deaths after January 1, 2001Montana DOR
Montana estate taxNone for deaths after 2004Montana DOR
Federal basic exclusion, year of death 2026$15,000,000IRS
Federal annual gift exclusion, 2026$19,000 per recipientIRS

An estate below the federal figure does not owe federal estate tax on that basis. Anyone who thinks an estate might approach the threshold should ask an estate attorney, since a house is only one asset in the total.

What taxes can still apply when heirs sell an inherited Montana home?

Income tax on the estate, income tax on any gain, and property tax are the three that remain. None of them is a death tax, but each can affect what the heirs net.

  • Fiduciary income tax: the estate's personal representative may need to file Montana Form FID-3 if a federal Form 1041 was filed and the decedent owned Montana property or had Montana-source income.
  • Capital gains: a sale for more than the basis produces a gain, discussed in the next section.
  • Property tax: the county still bills the house, and the first half and second half dates keep running during probate.

Our Montana capital gains guide covers the income tax rates in detail.

What is the tax basis of an inherited house in Montana?

The basis is generally the fair market value on the date the owner died. IRS Publication 551 lists the fair market value at the date of death as the usual starting point for property inherited from a decedent.

If you did not receive a Schedule A showing the estate tax value, the IRS says you can determine basis from the appraised value at the date of death for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes. Because Montana has no such tax, an independent appraisal is the practical way to document value.

Joint ownership and community property have special rules. When either spouse dies, the total value of community property generally becomes the basis of the entire property. Read Publication 551 closely if a surviving joint tenant or spouse held title with the decedent.

Who can sell the house, and how does probate affect that?

The personal representative can sell estate real estate once appointed, unless the will or a court order restricts it. Montana's Uniform Probate Code, MCA 72-3-613, says a personal representative acting reasonably for the benefit of interested persons may acquire or dispose of an asset, including land, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale.

The same section lets the representative make repairs, lease property, insure assets, pay taxes and assessments, and hire attorneys or agents. A restriction in a will or a formal-proceeding order can limit those powers, so a buyer or title company will want to see the letters of appointment.

The Montana Judicial Branch says state law provides for both informal and formal probate. The choice depends on the value of the estate and whether the decedent left a valid will. The court's self-help page offers a probate questionnaire, an affidavit of death, a small estate packet and a fiduciary statement.

How can a Montana house pass without probate?

Some houses transfer on death without a court case, and those transfers are recorded with a form. The Montana Realty Transfer Certificate lists transfers by operation of law, including termination of joint tenancy or a life estate by death and a transfer on death deed.

Type of transferDocuments the certificate asks you to attach
Termination of joint tenancy or life estate by deathCertified death certificate
Transfer on death deedRecorded transfer on death deed and certified death certificate
Court decreeCertified copy of the order or decree

The Judicial Branch page lists an optional form of transfer on death deed under MCA 72-6-415. Heirs who receive a house this way can sell it after recording, but they should have the title company review the chain of documents first.

What does property tax look like for an heir who does not live in the house?

The reduced rate for primary residences depends on someone living there. Under the Department of Revenue's 2026 structure, a primary residence qualifies for tiered rates of 0.76% on the first $378,000 of value, 0.90% to $756,000, 1.10% to $1,511,999 and 1.90% above that.

A property that is not a primary residence or a qualifying long-term rental falls under a flat 1.90%, a rate the department lists for second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots. An inherited house that sits empty during probate can therefore cost more in tax than it did while the owner lived there.

Unpaid property tax becomes delinquent with a 2% penalty and interest of 5/6 of 1% a month under MCA 15-16-102. The personal representative has power to pay taxes and assessments as an expense of administration, so paying on time is part of the job.

What documents do heirs need before listing or selling?

A title company will usually ask for proof of who has authority to sign. The checklist below is a common starting point, and your title officer may add items.

  • Certified death certificate.
  • Letters of appointment for the personal representative, or the recorded transfer on death deed.
  • A date-of-death appraisal to support the tax basis.
  • Current property tax bill and any delinquency notices.
  • A completed Realty Transfer Certificate, including the water right disclosure.

The certificate carries a $500 penalty, six months in jail, or both for filing an inaccurate or incomplete form, so accuracy matters even for a family transfer. Some transfers, such as a decedent's estate property or a termination of joint tenancy by death, are exceptions from providing sales price information.

When does a cash sale make sense for heirs?

A cash sale can suit heirs who live elsewhere, want to avoid repairs, or need to settle the estate quickly. It does not change the tax rules above, so the date-of-death basis, the property tax bill and the certificate filing all stay the same.

What it changes is the timeline and the repair burden. A house that needs a roof, a cleanout or an update can sell as-is, and the price will reflect the condition. Compare any offer against the costs of holding the house through probate, including taxes, insurance and utilities.

More questions about Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Montana have an inheritance tax?

No. The Montana Department of Revenue says the inheritance tax was repealed in November 2000 and does not apply to deaths after January 1, 2001.

Does Montana have an estate tax?

No. The department says Montana has no estate tax for deaths after 2004. The federal estate tax can still apply to very large estates, with a $15,000,000 basic exclusion for deaths in 2026.

Do heirs pay tax when they inherit a house in Montana?

Heirs do not owe a Montana death tax. They can owe income tax on a gain if they later sell for more than the date-of-death value, and they inherit the property tax bill.

Who can sell an inherited house in Montana?

The personal representative, subject to the will and any court order, has power under MCA 72-3-613 to sell estate real property at public or private sale.

Do I need probate to sell a house in Montana?

Not always. Montana allows informal and formal probate, and some houses pass by joint tenancy or a transfer on death deed. The title company decides what proof it needs.

Does the estate have to file a Montana income tax return?

Fiduciaries may need Form FID-3 if a federal Form 1041 was filed and the decedent owned Montana property or had Montana-source income.

What is the basis of inherited property?

Generally the fair market value at the date of death, per IRS Publication 551.

content:
Montana Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Montana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Montana Quitclaim Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Montana Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Montana Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Montana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Use of the word 'grant' in a conveyance implies only that the grantor has not previously conveyed the estate and that it is free from encumbrances made by the grantor or those claiming under the grantor. (70-20-304 MCA; source)
  • A deed transferring real property requires a Realty Transfer Certificate for recording, with exceptions for gifts and transfers between spouses or parent and child for nominal consideration. (15-7-305, 15-7-307 MCA; source)
  • A document not meeting 7-4-2636 standards costs the standard fee plus $10. (7-4-2637 MCA; source)
  • Beginning July 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue will adjust the recording fee biennially for inflation by rule. (7-4-2637 MCA; source)
Selling in Montana?
We buy Montana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is a quitclaim deed in Montana?

A Montana quitclaim deed is a written transfer of whatever interest the signer has in a piece of real property, with no promise that the interest is good. The Montana Judicial Branch publishes a one-page sample that reads "does hereby convey, release, remise, and forever quit claim" to the grantee, followed by the county, the property description, the words "together with the appurtenances," and a notary block.

That wording matters. Under 70-20-304, MCA, using the word "grant" in a conveyance implies two covenants: the grantor has not already conveyed the same estate to someone else, and the estate is free from encumbrances the grantor created or allowed. Those implied covenants can be sued on as if they were written into the deed. The court's quitclaim form is built around "quit claim" language instead, so a buyer should not assume the same assurances come with it.

In plain terms, a quitclaim passes the signer's share and stops there. If the signer owns the whole house, the buyer receives the whole house. If the signer owns half, or owns nothing, the deed passes half, or nothing.

What does a Montana quitclaim deed need before the county will record it?

The deed must be signed, acknowledged before a notary, printed to a few format rules, and filed with a Realty Transfer Certificate and the recording fee. The county clerk and recorder in the county where the land sits takes the filing.

The acknowledgment rule comes from 70-21-203, MCA: before an instrument can be recorded, its execution has to be acknowledged by the person signing it, or proved by a subscribing witness with notarized proof. The format rules are in 7-4-2636, MCA.

ItemWhat Montana law saysSource
AcknowledgmentSigner acknowledges before a notary, or execution is proved by a subscribing witness70-21-203, MCA
Paper and inkBlue or black ink on white paper, 8 1/2 x 11 or 8 1/2 x 14 inches7-4-2636, MCA
Margins3 inches at the top of page one, 1 inch at the top of later pages, 1 inch at the bottom, 1/2 inch on the sides7-4-2636, MCA
Parties and propertyNames of the parties on page one or two; a description of the property if the document conveys real property7-4-2636, MCA
Return addressName and mailing address of the person who gets the document back, upper left of page one7-4-2636, MCA
Transfer certificateRealty Transfer Certificate filed with the deed15-7-305, MCA

A notary's acknowledgment is exempt from the color and margin rules, and so is an embossed seal from the margin rules. Everything else on the page should follow them.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Montana?

For a standard document the recording fee is $20 for the first page and $10 for each additional page or fraction of a page. A deed that does not meet the 7-4-2636 format standards costs the standard fee plus $10. Both figures come from 7-4-2637, MCA.

  • A two-page standard deed: $20 plus $10, or $30.
  • A three-page standard deed: $40.
  • A two-page deed with a margin problem: $40, because of the extra $10.

The statute also changes the fee on a schedule. Beginning July 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue will set the fee by administrative rule, adjusting it every two years with a consumer price index factor based on June 2025. A deed recorded after that date may cost more than the figures above, so check the clerk and recorder's current fee sheet.

What is the Realty Transfer Certificate and when can the price be left off?

The Realty Transfer Certificate (Form RTC) is a Department of Revenue form that goes to the county clerk and recorder at the same time as the deed. The Department of Revenue says its purpose is to update property records quickly and to collect sale price information used in mass appraisal.

The names of the seller (grantor) and buyer (grantee) must be identical on the form and the deed. The form also asks for the last four digits of the Social Security or federal employer identification number of everyone in the transfer, and an Individual Taxpayer Identification number if a foreign national is involved.

A quitclaim between family members is where the exceptions matter. The certificate does not have to state the amount paid for these transfers:

  • A gift, or a transfer in contemplation of death without consideration.
  • A transfer between spouses, or between parent and child, for nominal consideration.
  • A transfer to a revocable living trust.
  • Property of a decedent's estate, and termination of joint tenancy or a life estate by death.
  • A transfer under a court decree, except a sheriff's sale.
  • A correction or supplement to a recorded instrument with no added consideration.

Transfer on death deeds work differently. Under Title 72, Chapter 6, Part 4, no certificate is needed when the deed is recorded. After the owner dies, the beneficiary files one with a copy of the recorded deed and a certified death certificate.

What does recording do for a quitclaim deed?

Recording puts the world on notice. Under 70-21-302, MCA, a conveyance that is acknowledged or proved, certified and recorded as the law prescribes is constructive notice of its contents to later purchasers and mortgagees from the moment it is filed with the county clerk.

The practical result is timing. A signed deed sitting in a drawer gives the grantee no public protection. If the grantor later signs a second deed or a mortgage to someone else, the person who recorded first is in the stronger position. The same statute lets a certified copy of a recorded conveyance be recorded in any other county with the same force as the original, which helps if a family owns land in more than one county.

Does a quitclaim deed trigger the due-on-sale clause on a mortgage?

It can. A due-on-sale clause lets a lender demand the full loan balance if all or part of the property is transferred without the lender's written consent, and federal law generally lets lenders enforce it.

Section 341 of the Garn-St Germain Act, 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3, protects some transfers on residential property with fewer than five dwelling units. A lender may not call the loan because of:

  • A transfer to a relative resulting from the death of the borrower.
  • A transfer where the borrower's spouse or children become an owner.
  • A transfer from a divorce decree, legal separation or property settlement that makes the spouse an owner.
  • A transfer into a living trust in which the borrower remains a beneficiary, if occupancy rights do not transfer.
  • A lease of three years or less without a purchase option.

A quitclaim to a friend, a business partner or an investor is not on that list. If the house has a mortgage, call the servicer before the deed is signed.

When does a quitclaim deed work, and when does it fall short?

A quitclaim works best when everyone already knows who owns the house and the goal is to change the name on title. It falls short when a buyer needs proof that title is clean.

  • Works well: adding or removing a spouse, moving the home into a revocable trust, a divorce settlement, a gift to a child, or releasing a co-owner's share.
  • Works poorly: a sale to an unrelated buyer who expects a title guarantee, a house with unknown heirs, or any property where liens may exist.

A quitclaim does not clear a lien. The Montana Legal Services Association explains that unpaid property tax becomes a tax lien, and the county cannot release it until the tax, interest and penalties are paid. Giving the house to a relative does not remove it.

Property tax class can change with the new owner too. For 2026 the Department of Revenue taxes primary residences and long-term rentals on a tiered scale starting at 0.76%, while second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay a flat 1.90%. A parent who deeds the family house to a child who will not live in it may be moving the property into a higher class.

What if the house is inherited, behind on payments, or needs repairs?

A quitclaim alone rarely solves those problems.

  • Inherited with several heirs: every heir with an interest has to sign, and any estate paperwork needs to be in order before a buyer will close.
  • Behind on mortgage or taxes: the debt stays attached to the property no matter who holds the deed.
  • Needs repairs: repairs do not affect how a deed works, but they do affect what a buyer will pay.

If you want to sell instead of retitle, a cash buyer can purchase the house as is, and the closing company handles the deed, the transfer certificate and the recording. Call or text us, or ask for a written cash offer on the form at the top of this page, with no obligation to accept.

More questions about Montana Quitclaim Deed

Is a quitclaim deed legal in Montana?

Yes. Montana recognizes quitclaim deeds, and the Montana Judicial Branch publishes a sample form. To be recorded, the deed must be acknowledged before a notary and filed with the county clerk and recorder along with a Realty Transfer Certificate and the recording fee.

How much does it cost to file a quitclaim deed in Montana?

The statutory recording fee for a standard document is $20 for the first page and $10 for each additional page. A document that does not meet the format standards costs $10 more. Starting July 1, 2027, the fee will be adjusted for inflation by Department of Revenue rule.

Do I need a notary for a Montana quitclaim deed?

Yes in practice. Before a deed can be recorded, its execution must be acknowledged by the signer, or proved by a subscribing witness with notarized proof, under 70-21-203, MCA.

Does a Montana quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?

No. Montana's implied covenants attach to the word "grant," and the court's quitclaim form uses "quit claim" language instead. The deed passes only what the signer owns and does not remove liens, unpaid taxes or other owners' interests.

Can a quitclaim deed make my lender call my mortgage?

It can if the lender has a due-on-sale clause and the transfer is not protected. Federal law protects transfers to a relative after the borrower's death, to a spouse or children, in some divorces, and into a living trust where the borrower stays a beneficiary. Other transfers are not on that list.

Montana Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Montana Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Montana Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Montana Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Montana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Montana taxes long-term capital gains at 3.0% and 4.1%; these rates remain for tax years 2026-2027, with brackets adjusted to match ordinary income. (HB337: 2026-2027 Montana Individual Income Tax Changes (MT DOR); source)
  • Tax year 2026 ordinary income rates are 4.7% and 5.65%; tax year 2027 rates are 4.7% and 5.4% (taxable income excludes long-term capital gains). (HB337 (MT DOR); source)
Selling in Montana?
We buy Montana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Montana tax capital gains when you sell a house?

Yes. Montana taxes net long-term capital gains as part of state income tax, and a house you owned for more than a year produces a long-term gain if you sold for more than your basis. The Department of Revenue says the rates stay at 3.0% and 4.1% for tax years 2026 and 2027.

The sources we reviewed show no separate real estate gains tax. The gain from your house goes on your Montana individual income tax return, Form 2, alongside your other income. A seller who qualifies for the federal home sale exclusion may owe little or nothing.

This page explains how the pieces fit. It is general information, so confirm your own numbers with the Department of Revenue or a tax professional.

What are the Montana capital gains rates and brackets?

There are two capital gains rates, 3.0% and 4.1%, and which one applies depends on how your gain compares with your Montana ordinary income. The Montana Department of Revenue's 2025 tables show the lower rate on the first slice of gain, minus ordinary income, and 4.1% above it.

Filing status (tax year 2025)3.0% applies to first4.1% applies to
Single or married filing separately$21,100 of gain, minus ordinary incomeGain above that
Married filing jointly or surviving spouse$42,200 of gain, minus ordinary incomeGain above that
Head of household$31,700 of gain, minus ordinary incomeGain above that

If your ordinary income already exceeds the threshold, all of your net long-term gain is taxed at 4.1%. For 2026 and 2027, House Bill 337 keeps the 3.0% and 4.1% rates but adjusts the brackets to match its new ordinary income ranges.

How do the 2026 and 2027 income tax changes affect a house sale?

House Bill 337 widens the lower ordinary income bracket and trims the upper rate, and it leaves the capital gains rates alone. Taxable income for these brackets does not include long-term capital gains, so the gain is taxed on its own schedule.

Tax yearSingleHead of householdMarried filing jointly
2026: 4.7% up to$47,500$71,250$95,000
2026: upper rate5.65%5.65%5.65%
2027: 4.7% up to$65,000$97,500$130,000
2027: upper rate5.4%5.4%5.4%

In 2025, by comparison, the upper ordinary income rate was 5.9%. The bill also raises the Montana earned income tax credit to 20% of the federal credit starting in 2026. The year of sale decides which table you use, so a December closing and a January closing fall under different brackets.

Do you owe federal tax on the gain from selling your Montana home?

Often not. If you sell your main home, you may exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 if you file jointly with your spouse. The IRS requires that you owned the home for at least 24 months and used it as a residence for at least 24 months within the five years before the sale.

  • The two years of ownership and two years of use can fall in different periods, as long as both are met inside the five-year window.
  • You generally cannot claim the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home during the prior two years.
  • If you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even when the gain is fully excluded.
  • Reporting uses Schedule D and Form 8949 when required.
  • Uniformed Services, Foreign Service and intelligence community members on qualified extended duty may suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years.

As an illustration of the arithmetic only: a single owner who meets both tests and has a $300,000 gain can exclude $250,000, leaving $50,000 to report. A married couple filing jointly could exclude the full $300,000. The IRS sale of your home topic and Publication 523 give the full rules.

What does the Montana Realty Transfer Certificate have to do with tax?

The certificate tells the state about your sale, and the state matches it to income tax returns. The Department of Revenue form says plainly that you may owe income taxes, because any gain on the transfer is Montana-source income that should be reported to the department.

The form asks for the last four digits of each seller's Social Security number or federal ID number, which the department uses to cross-match certificates with income tax returns. It also asks whether the property was your principal residence, defined as a dwelling occupied for at least seven months.

It must be filed with the county clerk and recorder when the deed is presented for recording. A false or missing form can bring a $500 penalty, six months in jail, or both.

The form lists distressed sales separately, with boxes for a sheriff's deed, trustee's deed, deed in lieu of foreclosure and short sale. It also has a box for transfers that are part of a 1031 or 1033 exchange.

How is your gain figured: basis, improvements and selling costs?

Your gain is the sale price minus your adjusted basis and the costs of selling. Basis starts with what you paid and rises with capital improvements, such as a new roof or an addition. Routine repairs do not add to basis.

Keep records that show:

  • The purchase price and closing statement from when you bought.
  • Receipts for improvements that added value or extended the life of the house.
  • The settlement statement from the sale, which lists commissions, title fees and any credits to the buyer.

Selling as-is means you do not spend money on fix-up work, and it also means you do not add to your basis before the sale. If your gain sits comfortably under the federal exclusion, that trade-off carries little tax cost. If you are near the limit, talk to a tax adviser before choosing.

What if you inherited the house or are selling soon after probate?

Inherited property usually gets a basis equal to its fair market value on the date of death. IRS Publication 551 states that the basis of inherited property is generally the fair market value at the decedent's date of death, which often removes most of the gain that built up during the owner's lifetime.

That means an heir who sells soon after inheriting often reports a small gain or none. Gifted property works differently, so read Publication 551 for your case.

Hold on to an appraisal or other date-of-death valuation. If you did not receive a Schedule A showing the estate tax value, the IRS says you can use the appraised value at the date of death for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes. Our Montana estate and inheritance tax guide covers the estate side.

What if you moved to Montana or sell from another state?

Montana's return gives a credit for income tax paid to another state or country on gains that Montana also taxes. The Department of Revenue's Schedule III includes a line for that credit on Montana net long-term capital gains, set at the lesser of the figures on its worksheet lines.

If you do not live in Montana but sell Montana real estate, the gain is still Montana-source income, as the certificate states. A nonresident seller should expect Montana to want it reported, and a title or escrow officer can tell you what paperwork applies to your closing.

How can a quick cash sale change your tax picture?

A cash sale does not change the tax rules, only the timing and certainty. The same federal exclusion, Montana rates and reporting forms apply whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan.

What you control is the paperwork. Selling costs reduce your gain, so ask for the settlement statement early and give it to your tax preparer.

Plan for the tax bill the following spring. Set aside part of your proceeds if you expect any gain above the exclusion, and keep the closing statement, the Realty Transfer Certificate copy and your basis records together.

More questions about Montana Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

What is the Montana capital gains tax rate?

Montana taxes net long-term capital gains at 3.0% and 4.1%. The Department of Revenue says those rates stay in place for tax years 2026 and 2027, with brackets adjusted to match the new ordinary income ranges.

Does Montana have a separate tax on selling a house?

No separate real estate gains tax appears in the sources we reviewed. The gain is reported on your Montana individual income tax return, Form 2, and you file a Realty Transfer Certificate with the county clerk and recorder at recording.

How much of my home sale gain is excluded?

Federal law lets you exclude up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home at least two of the last five years.

Do I owe Montana tax if I sell my primary home?

Only on gain that is not excluded. If your gain is fully excluded you may owe nothing, though you still report the sale if you receive a Form 1099-S.

Is capital gains tax collected at closing in Montana?

The sources we reviewed describe the gain as something you report on your income tax return for the year of sale, so plan to set money aside. Unpaid property tax, by contrast, is paid from proceeds at closing.

What is the basis of a house I inherited in Montana?

Generally it is the fair market value on the date of death, per IRS Publication 551. Keep a date-of-death appraisal so you can support it.

Where can I get Montana tax answers?

The Department of Revenue call center is (406) 444-6900, and its individual income tax page has forms and instructions.
